title: Integration Patterns for Government Services
objectives: Choose appropriate integration patterns for different government contexts
Understand the trade-offs between point-to-point, hub, API, messaging, and event-driven approaches
Design for synchronous and asynchronous integration scenarios
Navigate legacy integration challenges common in government
Handle data transformation and error management in integrations
whyThisMatters:
Government services don't exist in isolation. Every service you design will need to exchange data with other systems — departmental databases, cross-government platforms, external regulators, payment providers, identity services, and legacy systems that have been running since before some of your team were born. Integration is where government architecture projects most commonly fail, because the complexity of connecting systems is consistently underestimated.

The challenge isn't just technical. Government integration involves navigating different data standards across departments, working with systems that have no modern interfaces, handling data that crosses security boundaries, and coordinating with teams who have different priorities and timelines. Choosing the right integration pattern — and designing it to handle the inevitable failures — is one of the most consequential decisions you'll make as a Solution Architect.

content.heading: Integration Patterns: An Overview
content.body:
Integration patterns are proven approaches to connecting systems. Understanding the main patterns and their trade-offs helps you choose the right approach for each integration challenge.

**Point-to-Point Integration:**
Each system connects directly to every other system it needs to communicate with. Simple for two or three systems, but the number of connections grows exponentially — 5 systems need 10 connections, 10 systems need 45. In government, where the system landscape is large and constantly changing, point-to-point quickly becomes unmanageable.

Use when: You have a small number of systems with stable, well-defined interfaces. The integration is simple and unlikely to change.

Avoid when: You have many systems, the integration landscape is changing, or you need to transform data between systems.

**Hub-and-Spoke (Integration Hub):**
All systems connect to a central hub that routes, transforms, and orchestrates messages between them. Each system needs only one connection (to the hub) rather than connections to every other system. This simplifies the landscape but creates a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck.

Use when: You have many systems with different data formats that need to exchange data. The hub can handle the transformation and routing logic centrally.

Avoid when: The hub would become a bottleneck for high-volume, low-latency integrations. Also avoid when the hub becomes a political battleground — in government, the team that owns the hub gains significant power over other teams' ability to integrate.

**API-Based Integration:**
Systems expose their capabilities through well-defined APIs (typically REST or GraphQL). Other systems consume these APIs to access data or trigger actions. This is the dominant pattern for modern government services and aligns with the Technology Code of Practice's emphasis on open standards.

Use when: You need synchronous, request-response interactions. The data consumer needs specific data on demand. The API provider can handle the expected request volume.

Avoid when: You need to process large volumes of data in bulk, or when the consumer needs to react to changes in real-time without polling.

**Message-Based Integration:**
Systems communicate by sending messages through a message broker (queue or topic). The sender doesn't need to know who receives the message or when they process it. This decouples systems in time and space.

Use when: You need asynchronous processing, guaranteed delivery, or one-to-many communication. When the sender and receiver operate at different speeds or availability levels.

Avoid when: You need immediate responses, or when the added complexity of a message broker isn't justified by the integration requirements.

**Event-Driven Integration:**
Systems publish events when something significant happens ('application submitted,' 'payment processed,' 'decision made'). Other systems subscribe to events they're interested in and react accordingly. This is the most loosely coupled pattern and supports complex, evolving integration landscapes.

Use when: Multiple systems need to react to the same business events. The integration landscape is complex and changing. You want to minimise coupling between systems.

Avoid when: The overhead of an event infrastructure isn't justified by the complexity of the integration. For simple, bilateral integrations, events add unnecessary complexity.

content.heading: Synchronous vs Asynchronous: Choosing the Right Model
content.body:
The choice between synchronous and asynchronous integration is one of the most important decisions you'll make, and it's frequently made wrong in government projects.

**Synchronous integration** means the caller waits for a response. It's the natural model for user-facing interactions — the user clicks 'submit' and waits for confirmation. It's simple to understand and implement.

But synchronous integration creates tight coupling. If the downstream system is slow, your system is slow. If the downstream system is down, your system fails. In government, where you're often integrating with legacy systems that have unpredictable availability, synchronous integration can make your service fragile.

**Asynchronous integration** means the caller sends a request and continues without waiting for a response. The response arrives later, through a callback, a message, or a polling mechanism. This decouples the systems — your service doesn't fail when the downstream system is unavailable.

But asynchronous integration is more complex. You need to handle: messages that fail to deliver, messages that arrive out of order, duplicate messages, and the user experience of 'your request is being processed' rather than 'here's your answer.'

**Decision framework:**

Use synchronous when:
- The user needs an immediate response (eligibility check, payment confirmation)
- The downstream system is reliable and fast
- The interaction is simple (request-response)
- Failure of the downstream system should prevent the user from proceeding

Use asynchronous when:
- The processing takes time (document validation, complex calculations)
- The downstream system has variable availability or performance
- The interaction involves multiple steps or systems
- You want your service to remain available even when downstream systems are down
- You need guaranteed delivery (the message must eventually be processed)

**The hybrid approach:**

Many government services use a hybrid: synchronous for the user-facing interaction (accept the submission, return a reference number) and asynchronous for the back-end processing (validate the data, check against external systems, route to a caseworker). This gives users a responsive experience while allowing the back-end to handle complexity and unreliability gracefully.

For example, a grant application service might: synchronously accept the application and return a confirmation (fast, reliable), then asynchronously validate the applicant's details against Companies House (might be slow), check for duplicate applications (might be complex), and route to the appropriate caseworker (might involve business rules). The user sees 'Application received — we'll update you within 5 working days' rather than waiting for all the back-end processing to complete.

content.heading: Government Integration Platforms and Common Components
content.body:
UK government provides several common components and platforms that simplify integration. Using these is both a practical choice and a TCoP requirement ('share and reuse technology').

**GOV.UK Notify:** A notification service for sending emails, SMS messages, and letters. Instead of building your own email sending capability, integrate with Notify. It handles delivery, tracking, and the complexities of government email (branding, accessibility, Welsh language). Integration is via a simple REST API.

**GOV.UK Pay:** A payment processing service for taking payments from users. It handles PCI DSS compliance, card processing, and reconciliation. Integration is via REST API with webhooks for payment status updates.

**GOV.UK One Login:** The government's single sign-on service for citizen-facing services. Instead of building your own authentication, integrate with One Login. It handles identity verification, authentication, and account management.

**GOV.UK Forms:** A form-building service for simple data collection. For straightforward forms that don't require complex logic, Forms can replace custom form development entirely.

**Government Integration Hub (where available):** Some departments have integration hubs or API gateways that provide centralised routing, transformation, and security for integrations. Check whether your department has one before building point-to-point integrations.

**Cross-government APIs:** Various government systems expose APIs for common data: Companies House (company data), HMRC (tax data, with appropriate authorisation), Land Registry (property data), Ordnance Survey (geographic data). These are valuable data sources but each has its own authentication, rate limiting, and data quality characteristics.

**Practical considerations:**

Common components simplify your architecture but introduce dependencies. If GOV.UK Notify is down, your service can't send notifications. Design for this: queue notifications and retry, or have a fallback mechanism. Understand the SLAs of the common components you depend on and design your service's availability targets accordingly.

Also consider the limitations. GOV.UK Pay handles standard payment flows but may not support complex payment scenarios (split payments, recurring payments, refunds with conditions). GOV.UK Notify handles standard notifications but may not support complex personalisation or conditional logic. Understand the boundaries of each common component before committing to it.

content.heading: Legacy Integration Challenges
content.body:
In government, legacy integration is not an edge case — it's the norm. Most government departments have systems that are 10, 20, or even 30 years old, and your new service will almost certainly need to integrate with some of them.

**Common legacy integration challenges:**

*No API:* The legacy system was built before APIs were standard practice. Data access is through direct database queries, file exports, or screen scraping. Each approach has risks: direct database access bypasses business logic, file exports are batch-only, and screen scraping is fragile.

*Proprietary protocols:* The legacy system uses a proprietary communication protocol that requires specific client libraries or middleware. These libraries may not be available for modern platforms, creating a technology constraint.

*Batch-only processing:* The legacy system processes data in batches (typically overnight). If your service needs real-time data, you'll need to design around this constraint — perhaps caching the latest batch data and accepting that it's up to 24 hours old.

*Data format mismatches:* The legacy system uses data formats that don't match your service's data model. Field names are different, date formats are different, codes and classifications are different. Data transformation is needed, and it's more complex than it appears.

*Undocumented behaviour:* The legacy system behaves in ways that aren't documented. Error codes that aren't in the specification. Data validation rules that exist in the code but not in the documentation. Edge cases that nobody remembers implementing. You'll discover these during integration testing, not during design.

**Strategies for legacy integration:**

*The Anti-Corruption Layer:* Place an adapter between your service and the legacy system that translates between the two worlds. Your service talks to the adapter using modern protocols and data formats; the adapter talks to the legacy system using whatever it requires. This isolates your service from the legacy system's quirks and makes it easier to replace the legacy system later.

*The Strangler Fig Pattern:* Gradually replace legacy functionality by routing requests through a new system that delegates to the legacy system for features not yet migrated. Over time, more functionality moves to the new system until the legacy system can be decommissioned. This is less risky than a big-bang replacement.

*The Data Synchronisation Approach:* Rather than integrating in real-time, synchronise data between the legacy system and your service on a schedule. This avoids the complexity of real-time legacy integration but introduces data latency. Suitable when near-real-time data is acceptable.

*The API Wrapper:* Build a modern API layer in front of the legacy system that translates API calls into whatever the legacy system understands. This gives other systems a modern interface to work with while the legacy system remains unchanged. It's a pragmatic approach but adds a component that needs maintaining.

content.heading: Data Transformation and Mapping
content.body:
Data transformation is the unglamorous but critical work of converting data from one format to another as it flows between systems. In government, where different systems use different data standards, transformation is a significant part of every integration.

**Common transformation challenges:**

*Semantic differences:* Two systems use different terms for the same thing. One system calls it 'applicant,' another calls it 'claimant,' a third calls it 'customer.' The data is the same, but the labels are different. Mapping these semantic differences requires understanding both systems' data models.

*Structural differences:* One system stores an address as a single text field; another stores it as separate fields (line 1, line 2, city, postcode). Transforming between structures requires parsing and formatting logic that handles edge cases (addresses that don't fit the expected structure).

*Code differences:* One system uses 'M/F' for gender; another uses '1/2'; a third uses 'Male/Female/Other/Prefer not to say.' Mapping between code sets requires a reference data mapping that's maintained as either system's codes change.

*Temporal differences:* One system uses dates in DD/MM/YYYY format; another uses YYYY-MM-DD; a third uses Unix timestamps. Date transformation seems simple but is a common source of bugs, especially around time zones and daylight saving time.

*Completeness differences:* One system requires fields that another system doesn't collect. When data flows from the system with fewer fields to the system with more, you need a strategy for the missing data — default values, nullable fields, or a process to collect the missing information.

**Transformation design principles:**

1. **Transform at the boundary.** Don't scatter transformation logic throughout your service. Concentrate it in the integration layer (the anti-corruption layer or adapter) so it's easy to find, test, and maintain.

2. **Use a canonical data model.** Define a standard data model for your service and transform all external data to and from this model. This means each external system needs only one transformation (to/from the canonical model) rather than transformations to every other system.

3. **Handle errors gracefully.** Transformation will fail — data will be in unexpected formats, required fields will be missing, codes won't match. Design your transformation to handle these failures gracefully: log the error, skip the record (if appropriate), or queue it for manual review.

4. **Version your transformations.** External systems change their data formats. When they do, you need to update your transformation without breaking the integration. Version your transformation logic so you can support old and new formats during transition periods.

5. **Test with real data.** Transformation logic that works with sample data often fails with real data because real data contains edge cases that samples don't. Test with production-like data volumes and variety.

content.heading: Error Handling in Integrations
content.body:
Integration errors are inevitable. Systems go down, networks fail, data is invalid, timeouts occur. How you handle these errors determines whether your service is resilient or fragile.

**Types of integration errors:**

*Transient errors:* Temporary failures that resolve themselves — network blips, brief service outages, temporary overload. Strategy: retry with exponential backoff. Most transient errors resolve within seconds or minutes.

*Permanent errors:* Failures that won't resolve by retrying — invalid data, authentication failures, resource not found. Strategy: log the error, alert the appropriate team, and either fail gracefully (show the user a meaningful error message) or queue the request for manual intervention.

*Timeout errors:* The downstream system doesn't respond within the expected time. This could be transient (the system is slow) or permanent (the system is down). Strategy: set appropriate timeouts, retry once, then treat as a failure.

*Partial failures:* Some parts of a multi-step integration succeed while others fail. This is the hardest type to handle because you need to decide whether to roll back the successful parts, continue with partial data, or queue the failed parts for retry.

**Error handling patterns:**

*Circuit Breaker:* If a downstream system fails repeatedly, stop sending requests to it (open the circuit) and return a cached response or a graceful degradation. Periodically test whether the system has recovered (half-open the circuit). This prevents your service from being dragged down by a failing dependency.

*Dead Letter Queue:* Messages that can't be processed after multiple retries are moved to a dead letter queue for manual investigation. This prevents failed messages from blocking the processing of subsequent messages.

*Compensation:* When a multi-step process partially fails, execute compensating actions to undo the successful steps. For example, if a payment is processed but the notification fails, you might not need to reverse the payment — but you do need to ensure the notification is eventually sent.

*Idempotency:* Design integrations so that processing the same message twice produces the same result as processing it once. This is essential for retry logic — if a message is retried because the acknowledgment was lost, processing it again shouldn't create a duplicate record or a double payment.

**Government-specific error handling considerations:**

In government, integration errors can have serious consequences — a failed payment means a citizen doesn't receive money they're entitled to; a failed data submission means a business might miss a regulatory deadline. Design your error handling with these consequences in mind:

- Never silently drop data. Every failed integration should be logged, alerted, and eventually resolved.
- Provide meaningful error messages to users. 'Something went wrong' is not acceptable. 'We couldn't verify your company details — please try again in 30 minutes or call our helpline' is.
- Design for manual intervention. Some errors can't be resolved automatically. Provide tools for support staff to investigate and resolve failed integrations.
- Monitor error rates. A sudden increase in integration errors is an early warning of a problem. Set up alerting on error rates, not just individual errors.

content.heading: Designing Integration Architecture for Government
content.body:
Bringing together the patterns, challenges, and principles discussed in this lesson, here's a practical approach to designing integration architecture for government services.

**Step 1: Map the integration landscape.**
Identify every system your service needs to exchange data with. For each, document: what data is exchanged, in what direction, how frequently, what interface is available, and who owns the system. This is your integration inventory.

**Step 2: Classify each integration.**
For each integration, determine: Is it synchronous or asynchronous? Is it real-time or batch? Is it with a modern system (API available) or a legacy system (no API)? Is it within your department or cross-departmental? Is the data sensitive? This classification guides your pattern selection.

**Step 3: Choose patterns.**
For each integration, select the appropriate pattern based on the classification. Modern, synchronous, within-department: direct API call. Legacy, batch, cross-departmental: file transfer with transformation. High-volume, event-driven: message broker. Multiple consumers of the same data: event-driven with pub/sub.

**Step 4: Design the integration layer.**
Don't scatter integration logic throughout your service. Create a dedicated integration layer that handles: connection management, authentication, data transformation, error handling, retry logic, logging, and monitoring. This layer isolates your service from the complexity and unreliability of external systems.

**Step 5: Design for failure.**
For each integration, define: What happens when it fails? How is the failure detected? How is it communicated to users? How is it resolved? What's the fallback? Document these failure modes and test them.

**Step 6: Plan for change.**
Integrations change. External systems update their APIs. Data formats evolve. New systems are added. Design your integration layer to accommodate change without requiring changes to your core service. Use versioned APIs, configurable transformation rules, and feature flags for new integrations.

**Step 7: Monitor and measure.**
Instrument every integration with: request/response times, error rates, throughput, and availability. Set up alerting for anomalies. Review integration health regularly. Integration problems are often the first sign of wider system issues.

This systematic approach won't eliminate integration challenges — they're inherent in the government landscape — but it will ensure you're prepared for them and can manage them effectively.

workedExample.title: Integrating a New DESNZ Service with Three Legacy Systems
workedExample.context: DESNZ is building a new digital service for the Climate Change Agreements (CCA) scheme. The service needs to integrate with three existing systems: (1) A 15-year-old Oracle database that holds historical agreement data (no API, accessible only via database views), (2) The Environment Agency's emissions reporting system (SOAP API, batch processing overnight), (3) HMRC's Climate Change Levy system (REST API, but with strict rate limiting and a 4-week lead time for access approval).
workedExample.approach:
The SA designs an integration architecture that handles the different characteristics of each legacy system.

**Integration 1: Oracle historical database**
Pattern: Anti-corruption layer with data synchronisation.
Approach: Build a read-only API wrapper around the Oracle database views. The wrapper translates the legacy data model into the new service's canonical data model. Data is synchronised nightly to a read replica in the new service's infrastructure, so the new service never queries the Oracle database directly in real-time. This protects the legacy database from unexpected load and isolates the new service from Oracle availability issues.

Error handling: If the nightly sync fails, the new service uses the previous day's data and alerts the operations team. Users see a banner: 'Historical data may be up to 48 hours old.'

**Integration 2: Environment Agency emissions system**
Pattern: Asynchronous message-based integration.
Approach: The EA system sends emissions data as XML files via SFTP overnight. The new service picks up the files, transforms the XML to JSON using the canonical data model, validates the data, and loads it into the service database. A message queue handles the processing to ensure no data is lost if the transformation fails.

Error handling: Files that fail validation are moved to a dead letter queue. The operations team receives a daily report of failed files. The EA is notified of data quality issues through an agreed escalation process.

**Integration 3: HMRC Climate Change Levy system**
Pattern: Synchronous API with circuit breaker.
Approach: The new service calls HMRC's REST API to verify levy payment status when processing CCA applications. The API has strict rate limits (100 requests per minute), so the service implements request queuing and caching. A circuit breaker prevents the service from overwhelming HMRC's API during peak periods.

Error handling: If the HMRC API is unavailable, the circuit breaker opens and the service falls back to a cached response (levy status as of the last successful check). Applications that can't be verified are flagged for manual checking rather than rejected.

**Integration layer design:**
All three integrations are managed through a dedicated integration layer that provides: centralised logging (every integration call is logged with correlation IDs), monitoring (dashboards showing integration health, latency, and error rates), and configuration (connection details, retry policies, and transformation rules are configurable without code changes).
workedExample.outcome: The integration architecture handles the three very different legacy systems through appropriate patterns for each. The nightly sync with Oracle avoids real-time dependency on a fragile legacy database. The file-based integration with the EA works within their existing batch processing model. The API integration with HMRC respects their rate limits while providing a responsive user experience through caching. The integration layer provides operational visibility across all three integrations.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The key insight was that each integration required a different pattern. A one-size-fits-all approach (e.g., 'everything must be API-based') would have failed because the Oracle database has no API and the EA system only supports file transfer. The SA's value was in choosing the right pattern for each integration based on the specific characteristics and constraints of each legacy system, rather than imposing a uniform approach.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Integration That Nobody Owns
civilServiceScenario.background: During the development of a new DESNZ service, the team discovers that a critical integration — a data feed from the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) — has no clear owner. The integration was set up five years ago by a contractor who has since left. It runs as a scheduled task on a server that the DESNZ infrastructure team manages but doesn't monitor. The data feed provides licensing data that the new service needs, but nobody knows the data format specification, the error handling behaviour, or what happens when the feed fails.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You need to integrate with this data feed for the new service, but you can't rely on an integration that nobody understands, nobody monitors, and nobody maintains. You need to assess the integration, establish ownership, and either stabilise it or replace it.
constraints: The data feed has been running for 5 years without documented issues (but also without monitoring)
The NSTA has limited IT resources and a 3-month lead time for any changes to their systems
The new service needs the licensing data within 24 hours of it being updated at NSTA
The original contractor's documentation consists of a single page of notes
The scheduled task runs on a server that's scheduled for decommissioning in 6 months
Budget for integration work is limited — the programme didn't anticipate this complexity
The data includes commercially sensitive licensing information
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect who needs to resolve this integration challenge while keeping the programme on track.
civilServiceScenario.discussion: This scenario is extremely common in government — integrations that work but nobody understands. The temptation is to leave it alone ('if it ain't broke, don't fix it'), but the server decommissioning forces action. The approach should be: (1) reverse-engineer the current integration by examining the scheduled task, the data format, and the NSTA's system, (2) document what you find, (3) establish ownership (who is responsible for this integration going forward?), (4) design a replacement that's monitored, documented, and maintainable, (5) migrate to the new integration before the server is decommissioned.

practiceArtefact.description: For the CCA scheme service (from the worked example), produce an integration architecture document that covers: integration inventory, pattern selection rationale, data transformation approach, error handling strategy, and monitoring requirements.
practiceArtefact.guidance: For each integration, document: the systems involved, the data exchanged, the pattern chosen and why, the transformation required, the error handling approach, and the monitoring metrics. Use a consistent format so the document serves as both a design reference and an operational guide.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Integration Architecture: Climate Change Agreements Service**

**Integration Inventory:**
| # | Source | Target | Data | Direction | Frequency | Interface | Pattern |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Oracle Legacy DB | CCA Service | Historical agreements | Inbound | Nightly batch | DB Views | Data sync + API wrapper |
| 2 | EA Emissions System | CCA Service | Emissions reports | Inbound | Nightly batch | SFTP/XML | File-based + message queue |
| 3 | HMRC CCL System | CCA Service | Levy payment status | Bidirectional | On-demand | REST API | Sync API + circuit breaker |
| 4 | CCA Service | GOV.UK Notify | Notifications | Outbound | Event-driven | REST API | Async via queue |
| 5 | CCA Service | GOV.UK Pay | Payments | Bidirectional | On-demand | REST API | Sync API + webhooks |

**Pattern Selection Rationale:**

Integration 1 (Oracle): Data sync chosen because the Oracle DB has no API and cannot handle real-time queries from the new service. Nightly sync provides data freshness within 24 hours, which is acceptable for historical data. API wrapper provides a clean interface for the new service.

Integration 2 (EA): File-based chosen because the EA system only supports SFTP file transfer. Message queue added to ensure reliable processing — if transformation fails, the message is retained for retry rather than lost.

Integration 3 (HMRC): Synchronous API chosen because levy status is needed during application processing. Circuit breaker added because HMRC's rate limits and availability constraints require graceful degradation.

**Data Transformation:**
Canonical data model defined for the CCA service. Each integration has a dedicated transformer:
- Oracle: Maps legacy field names and codes to canonical model. Handles null fields in legacy data.
- EA: Transforms XML to JSON. Maps EA emissions codes to CCA scheme codes. Validates data completeness.
- HMRC: Minimal transformation — REST API returns JSON. Map HMRC status codes to CCA status values.

**Error Handling Strategy:**
| Integration | Transient Error | Permanent Error | Timeout |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oracle sync | Retry 3x with backoff | Alert ops, use previous day's data | 30-min timeout, alert if exceeded |
| EA file transfer | Retry pickup 3x | Dead letter queue, daily report | N/A (batch) |
| HMRC API | Retry 2x with backoff | Circuit breaker opens, use cached data | 10-sec timeout, fallback to cache |
| GOV.UK Notify | Retry via queue | Dead letter queue, manual resend | 30-sec timeout, queue for retry |
| GOV.UK Pay | Retry 1x | Alert ops, flag payment for manual processing | 15-sec timeout, show user error |

**Monitoring Requirements:**
- Dashboard showing: integration health (up/down), latency (p50, p95, p99), error rate, throughput
- Alerts for: integration failure, error rate > 5%, latency > 2x baseline, dead letter queue depth > 10
- Daily report: integration summary, failed records, data quality metrics
- Monthly review: integration performance trends, capacity planning

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the integrations in your current project. Are they designed with appropriate error handling, or do they assume the happy path?
How do you handle legacy systems that have no API? What patterns have you used successfully?
When was the last time an integration failure caused a significant problem? What would you design differently?
How well do you monitor your integrations? Would you know within minutes if an integration failed?
How do you handle data transformation between systems with different data models? Is your approach sustainable?

knowledgeCheck.question: When is point-to-point integration appropriate in a government context?
options: Always — it's the simplest pattern and should be the default
When you have a small number of systems with stable, well-defined interfaces
Only when integrating with legacy systems that don't support other patterns
Never — government services should always use an integration hub
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Point-to-point is appropriate for simple, stable integrations between a small number of systems. It becomes unmanageable as the number of systems grows (connections grow exponentially), but for two or three well-defined integrations, it's the simplest and most appropriate choice.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of the Anti-Corruption Layer pattern for legacy integration?
options: It makes the legacy system run faster
It isolates your service from the legacy system's data model and quirks, allowing independent evolution
It automatically converts legacy systems to use modern APIs
It prevents security vulnerabilities in the legacy system from affecting your service
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Anti-Corruption Layer translates between your service's data model and the legacy system's data model, isolating your service from the legacy system's quirks. This allows your service to evolve independently and makes it easier to replace the legacy system later.

knowledgeCheck.question: A government service needs to verify company details with Companies House during an application process. The Companies House API occasionally experiences 30-second response times. What integration pattern is most appropriate?
options: Synchronous API call with a 60-second timeout
Synchronous API call with a circuit breaker and cached fallback
Asynchronous verification with the user notified of the result later
Direct database connection to Companies House for faster access
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A circuit breaker with cached fallback provides the best balance: synchronous for normal operation (fast response), circuit breaker to prevent cascading failures when the API is slow, and cached data as a fallback so the user isn't blocked. Asynchronous would work but degrades the user experience unnecessarily for a usually-fast API.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is idempotency important in integration design?
options: It makes integrations faster by avoiding duplicate processing
It ensures that processing the same message twice produces the same result, which is essential for safe retry logic
It's a requirement of the Technology Code of Practice
It prevents unauthorised access to integration endpoints
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Idempotency ensures that retrying a failed message doesn't create duplicate records, double payments, or other unintended side effects. This is essential for reliable integration because messages may be retried when acknowledgments are lost or when transient errors occur.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should happen when an integration with a downstream system fails permanently during a user transaction?
options: Show the user a generic 'something went wrong' error and log the details
Silently retry indefinitely until the downstream system recovers
Show the user a specific, helpful error message and provide an alternative path (e.g., 'call our helpline')
Automatically roll back the entire transaction and ask the user to start again
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Users deserve specific, helpful error messages that explain what happened and what they can do about it. A generic error is frustrating and unhelpful. Silent infinite retry blocks the user. Automatic rollback loses the user's work. The best approach is a clear message with an alternative path forward.

practicalExercise.title: Designing Integration for a Multi-System Government Service
practicalExercise.scenario: You're designing a new DESNZ service for managing Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme (ESOS) compliance. The service needs to integrate with: (1) Companies House API (verify company details), (2) A legacy DESNZ database of previous ESOS submissions (Oracle, no API), (3) The Environment Agency's environmental permits system (SOAP web service), (4) GOV.UK Notify (send notifications), (5) A new DESNZ data warehouse (for policy analysis).
practicalExercise.task:
1. For each integration, recommend a pattern (synchronous API, asynchronous messaging, file transfer, data sync) with justification
2. Design the error handling approach for the two highest-risk integrations
3. Identify the integration that poses the greatest risk to the project and explain why
4. Propose a monitoring approach that gives the operations team visibility across all five integrations
hints: Consider the different characteristics of each system — modern API vs legacy vs internal
Think about which integrations are on the critical path for user transactions
Consider what happens to the user experience when each integration fails
Think about the data warehouse integration — it's different from the others because it's outbound
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**Integration Patterns:**

1. Companies House API: Synchronous API with circuit breaker and cache. Justification: User needs immediate verification during application. Companies House API is generally reliable but can be slow. Cache recent lookups to reduce API calls and provide fallback.

2. Legacy ESOS database: Nightly data sync with API wrapper. Justification: No API available, and historical data doesn't change frequently. Sync overnight to a read replica, expose through a clean API for the new service. Avoids real-time dependency on legacy Oracle.

3. EA environmental permits: Asynchronous via message queue. Justification: SOAP web service with variable response times. Permit verification isn't needed in real-time — queue the request, process asynchronously, update the application record when the response arrives.

4. GOV.UK Notify: Asynchronous via message queue. Justification: Notifications don't need to be sent synchronously with user actions. Queue notification requests for reliable delivery with retry.

5. DESNZ data warehouse: Event-driven outbound feed. Justification: The data warehouse consumes data from the service, not the other way around. Publish events (application submitted, assessment completed, compliance confirmed) that the data warehouse subscribes to and processes at its own pace.

**Error Handling for Highest-Risk Integrations:**

Legacy ESOS database (highest risk — no API, ageing infrastructure):
- Sync failure: Retry 3 times with exponential backoff. If all retries fail, alert operations team and continue using previous day's data. Display banner to users: 'Historical ESOS data may be up to 48 hours old.'
- Data quality issues: Validate all synced records against expected schema. Quarantine records that fail validation. Generate daily data quality report for operations.
- Infrastructure failure: If the Oracle server is unreachable for more than 24 hours, escalate to infrastructure team and programme manager. The new service continues to function with stale data.

Companies House API (critical path — blocks user application):
- Transient failure: Retry once after 2 seconds. If retry fails, check cache for recent lookup of the same company.
- Rate limiting: Implement request queuing to stay within rate limits. If queue depth exceeds threshold, show users a 'please try again in a few minutes' message.
- Extended outage: Circuit breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures. Service falls back to manual verification — application is accepted but flagged for caseworker to verify company details manually.

**Greatest Risk Integration:**
The legacy ESOS database poses the greatest risk because: (1) it has no API, requiring a custom sync mechanism, (2) the Oracle infrastructure is ageing and may have reliability issues, (3) nobody fully understands the data model, (4) data quality is unknown until we start syncing. Mitigation: invest in thorough data analysis before building the sync, and design the new service to function (with reduced capability) even when the legacy data is unavailable.

**Monitoring Approach:**
Centralised integration dashboard showing:
- Health status (green/amber/red) for each integration
- Latency metrics (p50, p95) for synchronous integrations
- Throughput and error rates for all integrations
- Queue depths for asynchronous integrations
- Data freshness for the legacy sync (time since last successful sync)
- Alerting: PagerDuty for critical failures (Companies House circuit breaker open, legacy sync failed for >24h), email for warnings (error rate >5%, queue depth >100)
assessmentCriteria: Pattern selection is justified by the specific characteristics of each system
Error handling addresses realistic failure scenarios with practical mitigations
Risk assessment identifies the most impactful integration challenge with clear reasoning
Monitoring approach provides actionable visibility across all integrations

commonMistakes: Assuming all integrations can be API-based when legacy systems don't support APIs
Designing only for the happy path — not considering what happens when integrations fail
Using synchronous integration for everything, creating tight coupling and fragile services
Underestimating the complexity of data transformation between systems with different data models
Not monitoring integrations — discovering failures only when users complain
Building point-to-point integrations that become unmanageable as the system landscape grows
Ignoring rate limits and overwhelming external APIs during peak periods
Treating integration as a development task rather than an architecture decision

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA designs all integrations as synchronous API calls, assuming every system has a modern API. When they discover the Oracle database has no API, they resort to direct database queries that bypass business logic. When the HMRC API is slow, the entire service slows down because there's no circuit breaker or caching. When the EA file transfer fails, nobody notices for three days because there's no monitoring. Integration problems consume 60% of the operations team's time.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA assesses each integration individually and chooses the appropriate pattern for each. Legacy systems get anti-corruption layers and data sync. Unreliable APIs get circuit breakers and caching. File transfers get message queues and dead letter queues. Every integration is monitored with alerting. When problems occur, they're detected within minutes and resolved through documented procedures. Integration is reliable and the operations team spends their time on improvement, not firefighting.
